stem: $EFGH$ is a parallelogram with vertices $E({=e_x}, {=e_y})$, $F({=f_x}, {=f_y})$ and $G({=g_x}, {=g_y})$. Find the coordinates of $H$ by using the fact that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
solution: Since the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, the mid-point of $EG$ is equal to the mid-point of $FH$. First find the mid-point of $EG$, then use it together with $F$ to find the coordinates of $H$.
notes: Basic-tier entry point of the skill: the parallelogram is fully named (EFGH) with three vertices given in text, no diagram, mirroring q:g10m8s4-1-3:ex8-6-23's own template exactly (verified against its literal numbers: e_x=-1,e_y=2,f_x=-2,f_y=-1,g_x=2,g_y=0 reproduces H(3,3)). Diagonals are the 'skip-one' pairs EG and FH, the same fact the book's other five questions on this objective use (ex8-6-31e, ex8-6-36a uses a different, non-bisecting method and was therefore not used as a parent; we13, ex8-6-38e, ex8-6-46e all use this same bisecting method). Only the non-collinearity constraint is enforced, so the EG midpoint is sometimes a whole number and sometimes a genuine fraction (as in the book's own worked example, 1/2) — both are honest basic-tier outcomes since H itself is always a whole-number pair by construction (h_x = e_x+g_x-f_x has no division). signed(g_x)/signed(g_y) avoid a double sign such as '-1+-3' when the second addend is negative; f_x+x and f_y+y never need signed() since the second term is the literal unknown letter, not a signed number. Numeric range kept to [-6,6] to stay in the book's own magnitude (its examples range roughly -3 to 11) and avoid oversized coordinates for a first exposure to the skill. Answer type is 'expression'/coordinates rather than mcq: there is no natural finite set of plausible alternatives to choose from here (any error just produces a different, equally 'plausible-looking' wrong pair), so typing the pair is the honest format, consistent with the rule against using mcq to dodge typing. No new misconceptions were needed — the three already catalogued (diagonal-vs-side-confusion, midpoint-formula-subtraction, shared-midpoint-as-vertex) all describe numeric-answer errors a reviewer can recognise directly in a wrong (h_x, h_y) submission without needing a distractor list.
